title: Engineering Coherence and Ergotropy through Spatial Arrangement of Environmental Channel in a Two-Qubit Quantum Battery
abstract: We investigate how the spatial arrangement of environment channel influences the dynamics of coherence and work extraction in a two-qubit quantum battery with resonant qubits coupled through an XY-exchange interaction. Qubit B is attached to a finite-temperature thermal bath, while RTN noise is applied either to qubit A or to qubit B, depending on whether it is in a separated or co-located configuration, respectively. Two complementary product states are considered to initialise the coherence on different qubits. The dynamics are evaluated using local $l_{1}$-norm coherence, global ergotropy and the global-local ergotropy gap. The results suggest that a stronger exchange interaction enhances the redistribution of coherence without necessarily improving retention of extractable work. For the parameter investigated, the greater global ergotropy is retained in the case of the co-located configuration, especially when the initially coherent qubit is not directly affected by the RTN. However, the configuration provides the largest global-local ergotropy gap, which varies with the exchange interaction, initial state and thermal coupling. Suppression of the gap at large $J$ is typically observed in the case of stronger thermalisation, although enhancement of intermediate-coupling may occur. These results establish that total extractable work, local coherence and collective work advantage quantify the distinct aspects of quantum battery performances. The initial distribution of coherence and the spatial arrangement thus provide complementary mechanisms for regulating locally and collectively extractable work in interacting open quantum batteries.
summary: This paper analyzes a two-qubit quantum battery to determine how coupling the qubits to the environment affects energy storage and coherence. By comparing 'separated' versus 'co-located' environmental noise channels, the authors show that the optimal setup depends on whether one prioritizes total extractable work or the advantage gained from collective operations. This highlights environmental placement as a key control knob for quantum device performance.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spatial arrangement of environmental coupling channels influences the dynamics of coherence and the extractable work (ergotropy) in a two-qubit quantum battery.
main_result: The optimal environmental configuration (separated vs. co-located) depends on the initial coherence distribution and the specific performance metric (e.g., global ergotropy vs. global-local gap).
method: The dynamics are analyzed using master equations incorporating thermal baths and Random Telegraph Noise (RTN), evaluating coherence via $l_1$-norm and work extraction via global and local ergotropy.
model_or_system: The system is a two-qubit quantum battery coupled by an XY-exchange interaction, subjected to environmental noise modeled by a Lindblad master equation and RTN terms. Two configurations are compared: separated (RTN on A, bath on B) and co-located (both on B).
key_observables: Local $l_1$-norm coherence, global ergotropy (extractable work), and the global-local ergotropy gap.
important_parameters: Exchange interaction strength ($J$), thermal coupling ($\kappa$), initial coherence location, and the specific environmental configuration.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on weak-coupling approximations for the thermal bath.
figures_summary: Figures compare the dynamics of local coherence and the maximum global-local ergotropy gap ($\Delta W_{	ext{max}}$) as a function of the exchange interaction strength ($J$) for different initial states and thermal couplings.
paper_structure: The paper models the system dynamics using master equations for two distinct environmental placements (separated vs. co-located) and analyzes the evolution of coherence and work extraction using multiple diagnostics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system control, showing how engineering the coupling to the environment can be a tunable resource to optimize quantum battery performance for specific tasks.
